plan.contextChunk: This figure is a plane diagram in which one ellipse is shown against two superimposed coordinate systems. The standard frame consists of thin black double-headed arrows, a horizontal axis labeled x at its right end and a vertical axis labeled y at its top, meeting at the origin. Laid over them is a second pair of orange double-headed axes rotated counterclockwise about that same origin: the one running from lower left to upper right is labeled x', and the one running from lower right to upper left is labeled y'. The ellipse is a dark blue outline centered at the origin and tilted so that its long axis lies along the orange x'-axis and its short axis along the y'-axis; it crosses the black horizontal axis on both sides and extends above and below the black vertical axis. A small curved arc drawn between the positive x-axis and the positive x'-axis marks the rotation and is labeled theta. Neither set of axes carries tick marks or numeric values. Placing both frames on one picture invites a comparison between a point's coordinates in the original system and its coordinates in the rotated one. The figure motivates the treatment of conic equations that contain an xy term, which describe conics turned away from alignment with the coordinate axes.

interactionPlan.concept: A conic that is tilted relative to the standard x,y axes carries an xy cross-term in its equation; rotating the coordinate frame by the tilt angle theta aligns the axes with the conic's principal axes and makes that cross-term vanish.

orange rotated y'-axis as a thicker double-headed arrow running lower-right to upper-left, labeled 'y'
dark blue ellipse outline centered at the origin, long axis along x' and short axis along y'

equation panel showing the general conic in x,y with the Bxy cross-term
equation panel showing the same conic in x',y' with no cross-term
clickable point marker on the ellipse

coordinate readout (x', y') in the rotated frame

interactions.label: Rotation angle theta
interactions.teaches: Dragging theta turns the orange x',y' frame and the ellipse together while the black x,y frame stays fixed, so the learner sees the rotation that realigns the axes with the conic and thereby removes the visual misalignment behind the xy term

interactions.label: Equation frame
interactions.teaches: Switching frames highlights the active axes and the matching equation together: in x,y the Bxy cross-term is present and emphasized, while in x',y' that term disappears, showing exactly why the rotated frame simplifies the conic

Clicking a point on the ellipse draws its projections onto both axis systems and shows two coordinate readouts, making concrete that one physical point has different numeric coordinates in the original frame versus the rotated frame

demo_steps.title: Tilted conic, misaligned axes
demo_steps.narration: The ellipse's long axis lies along the orange x' direction, not the black x-axis, so in the standard frame its equation needs an xy cross-term. The theta arc records the misalignment angle.

demo_steps.title: Rotate the frame
demo_steps.narration: Drag theta and watch the orange axes and ellipse turn as a rigid pair about the origin while the black axes stay put — the rotation is what carries the conic into alignment with a coordinate frame.

demo_steps.title: Cross-term vanishes
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the x',y' equation: the highlighted Bxy term is gone and only squared terms remain, because the rotated axes now run along the ellipse's principal axes.

demo_steps.title: Same point, two coordinates
demo_steps.narration: Click any point on the ellipse: dashed projections drop to both axis pairs and two readouts appear, confirming the point is unchanged in space but its coordinates differ between the two frames.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The xy cross-term is not a property of the conic itself but of the choice of axes — rotating the frame by the tilt angle theta aligns the axes with the conic's principal axes and eliminates the cross-term.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Center the figure on the origin. Draw the standard frame as thin black double-headed arrows (x right, y up) with no ticks. Overlay the rotated frame as thicker orange double-headed arrows (x' lower-left to upper-right, y' lower-right to upper-left) that rotate live with the slider. Draw the ellipse as a clean dark-blue outline centered at the origin, its major axis locked to x' and minor axis to y', so it visibly tilts as theta changes. Add a small curved arc with an arrowhead between the positive x-axis and positive x'-axis labeled theta. Place the equation panel to one side: in the x,y view show 'Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 = F' with the Bxy term colored red/emphasized; in the x',y' view show 'A'x'^2 + C'y'^2 = F' with no cross-term, and tint the matching axes to link equation to frame. On click, render a filled marker on the ellipse plus light dashed perpendiculars to all four axes and two small coordinate labels (x,y) in black and (x',y') in orange. Cross-fade equation panels and projection sets rather than hard-cutting.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for rotating the coordinate frame by theta: the learner drags theta, the orange x' and y' axes turn with the ellipse while the black x and y axes stay fixed, showing how rotation removes the visual misalignment behind an xy term.
- Toggle between original and rotated equations: the learner switches from the x,y equation with the xy term to the x',y' equation aligned to the ellipse, and the active axes and equation terms highlight together to show why the rotated frame simplifies the conic.
- Click for coordinate comparison at a point: the learner clicks a point on the ellipse, projections to both axis systems appear with two coordinate readouts, making clear that the same point has different coordinates in the two frames.

authoredContext:
Until now, we have looked at equations of conic sections without an xy term, which aligns the graphs with the x- and y-axes. When we add an xy term, we are rotating the conic about the origin. If the x- and y-axes are rotated through an angle, say θ, then every point on the plane may be thought of as having two representations: (x,y) on the Cartesian plane with the original x-axis and y-axis, and (x ′, y ′) on the new plane defined by the new, rotated axes, called the x'-axis and y'-axis. See the figure.

The graph of the rotated ellipse x 2 + y 2 –xy–15=0

An ellipse centered at the origin, aligned with a rotated coordinate system (x', y') that is at an angle θ with respect to the standard (x, y) coordinate system.

We will find the relationships between x and y on the Cartesian plane with x ′ and y ′ on the new rotated plane. See the figure.

discrepancies: The source figure contains no equation text, but the generated figure overlays a large equation string ('2.03x² + -2.06xy + 2.03y² = 30625') in the top-left of the plot area, altering the clean composition of the original.
The cross-term is rendered as '+ -2.06xy' (a plus sign immediately followed by a negative coefficient) instead of a properly formatted '− 2.06xy'.
The equation's right-hand side is the unnormalized '= 30625' rather than the conventional '= 1' for a conic, which looks like a raw scaling artifact.
The ellipse stroke is a darker navy (#1a3a6b) than the medium blue used in the source.
evaluation.notes: The rotated ellipse, black axes, orange x'/y' axes, and θ arc all match the source in orientation, proportion, and color, and the interactions (θ slider rotating the rigid ellipse+frame pair, equation-frame toggle, step player, and click-to-compare projections) are functional and conceptually correct; the main weaknesses are cosmetic — an added equation overlay with an awkward '+ -2.06xy' sign and an unnormalized '= 30625' right-hand side.
action_items: Format the cross-term sign correctly: when B is negative, emit '− |B|xy' (and drop the preceding '+') instead of concatenating '+ ' with a negative number to produce '+ -2.06xy'.
Normalize the displayed conic equation to '= 1' (divide A, B, C by F) or otherwise present coefficients in standard form rather than the raw '= 30625'.

Move the equation readout out of the plot area (e.g., into the right-hand UI panel) so the default state reads as a clean drop-in for the source image, and lighten the ellipse stroke toward the source's medium blue.
